forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire to bring in new special school funding bands from the autumn 2026 term
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire's special schools will be funded under a new banding model from the autumn 2026 term, according to papers for the county's Schools' Forum meeting on 8 October. Banding sets the funding a school receives according to the level of need among its pupils.

The papers, an update on reforms to support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), say the review of the framework has been "progressed and concluded". The new model was developed with special school leaders and finance colleagues. It is meant to line funding up more closely with need, so that banding and funding "more accurately reflect need from the outset".

A key aim, the paper says, is to reduce reliance on exceptional funding arrangements, those that sit outside the standard bands. It also links the change to the long-term financial sustainability of the High Needs Block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The papers give no figures for what the new model will cost or save.

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire schools grant overspent by £23.0m in 2025/26, pushing its reserve negative for first time
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council overspent its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £23.0 million in 2025/26, according to a value for money risk assessment before its Audit Committee on 21 September. The year was the first in which the grant's reserve moved into a negative position.

The paper attributes the overspend principally to the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. It says this reflects "a continued increase in the number of children and young people requiring specialist educational support and services." The paper describes the deficit as a structural demand pressure that persists, rather than a one-year variation.

The council has set up arrangements to review how effective its high needs spending is. The paper does not give a figure for the total deficit now carried on the grant, a date by which the overspend is expected to stop, or the amount the review is expected to save.
news_drafts.paper_title: VFM risk assessment - Lincolnshire County Council

news_drafts.headline: Lincolnshire County Council's schools grant overspent by £13.406m in 2025-26, leaving a £25.005m deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Lincolnshire County Council overspent its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £13.406m in 2025-26, according to its review of financial performance for the year. Excluding school balances, the paper puts the deficit carried forward at £25.005m, which it describes as structural.

The paper attributes the overspend to "continued pressure within the High Needs block". High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities.

The paper says government will support approximately 90% of deficits to 31 March 2026, but only if the council submits an approved plan for reforming support for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). Any amount the government does not cover must be managed through the council's future financial planning, the paper says.

The papers given to the desk do not say how much of the £25.005m the 90% would cover, or when the council expects to submit its SEND reform plan.

findings.headline: SEND specialist education placement provision costing £36.130m for 696 children, with external specialist placement funding overspending by £2.669m
findings.detail: The council maintained 696 children in specialist education placements costing £36.130m at the end of March 2026. External SEND specialist placements overspent by £2.669m due to increased demand for pupils with complex needs where mainstream schools cannot meet their needs. Special school top-up funding also overspent by £1.785m to meet increasing severity of need.
findings.matters: The scale and growth of specialist SEND provision costs are material to overall council finances; lenders and peer finance officers need to understand demand trajectory and how costs are funded
findings.figures: £36.130m for 696 children; £2.669m external specialist placement overspend; £1.785m special school top-up overspend
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026 there were 696 children in specialist education placements costing £36.130m. External SEND specialist placements have overspent by £2.669m due to an increase in demand for those pupils with complex needs, where mainstream schools cannot meet need.

findings.headline: EHC plan funding overspent by £10.709m (25.9% of budget), with Lincolnshire's rate 15 per cent above national and 30 per cent above regional average
findings.detail: Top-up and targeted funding for children with Education and Health Care plans overspent by £10.709m (25.9% of budget). Lincolnshire's EHC plan rate of 6.1% of the school population significantly exceeds both national average (15% higher) and regional average (30% higher). The EHC plan growth rate increased 10% from the prior year.
findings.matters: This reveals structural SEND identification and funding patterns significantly above peer councils, signalling systemic challenges in mainstream inclusion that peers should assess
findings.figures: £10.709m overspend (25.9% of budget); 6.1% EHC plan rate; 15% above national, 30% above regional average; 10% growth from prior year
findings.quote: Lincolnshire's EHC plan rate was 6.1% of the school population in 2025 which was 15% higher than national and 30% higher than the regional average. The EHC plan growth rate increased by 10% from the prior year adding further pressure to the system.

findings.headline: Council budgeted for £18.492m planned overspend on High Needs block in 2025/26
findings.detail: The council set its High Needs budget with a built-in planned overspend of £18.492m in 2025/26. Beyond this, the paper details an additional £11.567m in overspend driven by demand-led services: EHC plan funding (£10.709m), external specialist placements (£2.669m), and special school top-up funding (£1.785m), partly offset by underspends in alternative provision (£3.596m).
findings.matters: A budgeted structural overspend signals funding inadequacy in High Needs provision; finance directors and lenders need to understand how such overspends are funded and whether they are sustainable
findings.figures: £18.492m planned overspend; £30.059m total High Needs overspend; £11.567m additional overspend beyond planned
findings.quote: Even allowing for the careful management of the DSG, a focus on early intervention and transformation, and a strong financial position compared to many LAs, the Council set a budget based on a planned overspend on its High Needs block funding allocation of £18.492m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Mainstream Schools Funding Consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: Affordability gap from lagged government funding requires continued sector-wide downward AWPU adjustment for 2027/28, following -0.612% reduction in 2026/27
findings.detail: An affordability gap arises because government allocates funding based on lagged pupil data: 2026/27 funding uses October 2024 census figures while councils must fund schools using the current year census (October 2025). Lincolnshire has experienced significant growth in Free School Meals and FSM Ever 6 entitlements from pandemic effects and cost-of-living pressures. In 2026/27, the council made a -0.612% downward adjustment to Age Weighted Pupil Unit (AWPU) values across the sector to address the gap. The council proposes to continue this approach for 2027/28, with 84% of responding schools supporting the sector-wide solution.
findings.matters: This represents a structural mismatch between government funding methodology and actual pupil demand that will require ongoing annual mitigation, revealing where the council's budget pressures originate and how schools funding sustainability depends on recurring sector-wide adjustments.
findings.figures: -0.612% AWPU adjustment in 2026/27; 84% of schools support continuing sector-wide AWPU adjustment approach for 2027/28
findings.quote: Lincolnshire has seen significant growth in both FSMs and FSMs Ever 6 over the years, firstly from the pandemic and latterly with the cost-of-living challenges, which has caused these affordability gaps.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Mainstream Schools Funding Consultation 2027-28
findings.headline: High Needs block projected overspend of £51.947m in 2026/27 with third annual proposal to transfer 0.5% of Schools block drawing only 31% school support
findings.detail: The council's latest forecast for 2026/27 shows a projected High Needs block overspend of £51.947m. The council is proposing a 0.5% transfer of Schools block funding to High Needs block for the third consecutive year to support SEND initiatives. Only 9 of 22 responding primary schools (41%) and 2 of 9 responding secondary schools (22%) support the proposal. Schools opposing the transfer cite ongoing financial pressures and concern that transferring funds would reduce mainstream schools' capacity to deliver early intervention and support for pupils' needs.
findings.matters: A finance director watching peers is interested in whether a council can build consensus on mitigation measures for structural overspends; the limited support (31% overall) signals difficulty in securing stakeholder agreement on sustainable solutions.
findings.figures: £51.947m High Needs projected overspend in 2026/27; 41% of primary schools support transfer, 22% of secondary schools support transfer; third annual proposal
findings.quote: The latest forecast for 2026/27 indicates a projected overspend of £51.947m.

daily_post.headline: Government imposed two-unitary LGR against council's single-unitary preference
daily_post.lead: LGR is a structural change affecting finances, governance and service continuity; councils' preferences being overridden creates execution risk and potential unexpected costs during transition that a lender must account for.
